question: Why does Jupiter have so many moons?
shortAnswer: Gravity’s reach grows with mass, and Jupiter has more of it than anything in the solar system except the Sun. A wide region around it is a place where a small body stays with Jupiter instead of orbiting the Sun on its own.
title: Why Does Jupiter Have So Many Moons?
description: Jupiter’s mass gives it a huge gravitational reach, so dozens of small bodies stay bound to it instead of orbiting the Sun alone.
graphicCaption: Four large inner moons — Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto — on nested paths. The picture is not to scale in distance; it is a family portrait.
graphicAlt: Jupiter with four nested circular moon orbits, labelled as not to scale.

sections.heading: A planet that acts like a small system
body: The same falling-and-missing that keeps Earth beside the Sun keeps Io beside Jupiter. More mass means a stronger pull at any distance, and so a larger volume of space where “beside Jupiter” beats “beside the Sun.” Jupiter has more mass than every other planet combined — its keep-a-moon region is correspondingly enormous.

sections.heading: Four worlds you can see for yourself
body: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto formed from a disc around young Jupiter, the way the planets formed from a disc around the Sun — a solar system in miniature. Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury. All four show in steady binoculars as pinpricks in a line beside the planet, shifting night to night; watching them move is how Galileo proved not everything orbits Earth, and you can repeat the observation from a backyard.

sections.heading: Captured crowds and a moving count
body: Beyond the four giants, the census is mostly captured asteroids on distant, tilted, often backwards orbits — snatched from the belt Jupiter itself stirs. Counting “how many moons” is then a census of what telescopes can currently see, not a closed number, which is why the figure in the news keeps changing. Saturn’s count climbs for exactly the same reason.

seeItLive.label: Zoom to Jupiter’s moons

question: Why is the night sky dark?
shortAnswer: If stars went on forever, every line of sight would hit a star and the night would be as bright as a surface of suns. It is not. The dark is a clue that the universe is not an infinite, unchanging hall of lights.
title: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
description: Olbers’ paradox: an infinite, eternal star field would make night as bright as day. The dark sky means that picture is wrong.
graphicCaption: Each shell of stars at a greater distance has more stars, but each star looks smaller. In an endless steady universe those shells would add up to a wall of light. They do not.
graphicAlt: Concentric shells of stars around an observer, illustrating Olbers’ paradox.

sections.heading: The puzzle is older than the answer
body: People noticed the puzzle long before anyone had a Big Bang. Dust does not save you: dust would heat until it glowed too. The way out is that we cannot see forever in time. Light has a starting gun, and most lines of sight run out of time before they run into a star.

sections.heading: Expansion makes it darker still
body: Space stretching while light is in flight also drops the energy of distant starlight. The dark is then two facts together: a finite age, and an expanding space. Either one would dim the sky; we have both.

seeItLive.label: The glossary

question: What is a synodic month?
shortAnswer: A synodic month is the time from one full moon to the next, about 29.5 days. It is longer than the Moon’s trip around Earth relative to the stars, because Earth has moved and the Moon must catch up to the same angle with the Sun.

teasers./: Full moon to full moon is about 29.5 days, a little longer than one trip around Earth.
teasers./earth/: The simulator's month and the calendar month are not the same length, and that difference is this.

title: What Is a Synodic Month?
description: The synodic month is full moon to full moon, about 29.5 days — longer than the 27.3-day sidereal month.
graphicCaption: One lap around Earth relative to the stars is not yet the same phase. The Sun’s direction has shifted because Earth moved.
graphicAlt: Moon orbiting Earth with the Sun’s direction shifting as Earth orbits.

sections.heading: Two months, one Moon
body: Sidereal month: back to the same stars, about 27.3 days. Synodic month: back to the same phase, about 29.5 days. Calendars and the word “month” follow the phases, so they follow the longer one.

sections.heading: Why moonrise slips
body: Earth must turn extra to catch the Moon, which has moved east. That extra is about 50 minutes a day — the same arithmetic as the synodic month spread over 24 hours.

seeItLive.label: Scrub one synodic month

question: What is tidal locking?
shortAnswer: The Moon keeps the same face toward Earth because it turns once in the same time it goes around us. That match is tidal locking — not a dark side that never sees the Sun.

teasers./: The same face stays toward us because the Moon turns once per orbit.
teasers./earth/: The near-side drawing on the moon card is not a choice of illustration. The far side never shows.

title: What Is Tidal Locking?
description: Tidal locking is a spin matching an orbit, so one face stays toward the planet. The Moon’s far side still has day and night.
graphicCaption: A mark on the Moon stays aimed at Earth all the way around. The Sun still lights the left half of the ball. The far side has plenty of daytime.
graphicAlt: Moon with a marked near side facing Earth as it orbits, while the Sun lights one half.

sections.heading: Far side is not dark side
body: The far side is the hemisphere we never see from Earth. The dark side is whatever hemisphere is in night right now. They coincide only at full moon, when we are looking at the whole lit face — the “dark side” question has its own page because the answer surprises almost everyone.

sections.heading: One spin per lap, exactly
body: Locked does not mean not spinning. The Moon rotates — once per orbit, exactly, which is the one rate that holds a face still toward a moving Earth. Walk around a chair while always facing it and you have done the same thing: one full turn of your body per lap, without ever showing the chair your back. And the lock is almost perfect rather than perfect — the orbit’s slight ellipse lets the Moon rock a few degrees, so we see about 59% of it over time.

sections.heading: How the match was forced
body: Earth’s tides in the Moon’s solid body lagged the bulge, torqued the spin, and bled rotational energy until the periods matched. The same kind of torque is still running: it pushes the Moon a few centimetres farther out each year and slowly lengthens our day. Tidal locking is the normal fate of close moons — nearly every large moon in the solar system shows its planet one face.

seeItLive.label: Watch one face stay aimed at Earth

question: What is libration?
shortAnswer: Libration is a small wobble in the Moon’s facing. We still have one near side, but over time we see about 59% of the surface, not 50%. The extra is a peek around the edges.
title: What Is Libration?
description: Libration is the Moon’s apparent wobble, letting us see about 59% of its surface over time even though it is tidally locked.
graphicCaption: A locked Moon on an ellipse seems to nod: the spin is steady, the orbital speed is not, so we look slightly around the east or west limb.
graphicAlt: Moon disc with a slight rotation showing a sliver of the far-side limb.

sections.heading: A peek, not a roll
body: If the orbit were a perfect circle and we sat at the centre, tidal locking would show us exactly half. The orbit is a little stretched, and we are a little off to the side on a turning Earth. Those geometric cheats are libration.

sections.heading: Three small cheats
body: Longitudinal: the Moon speeds up near perigee while its spin stays even. Latitudinal: the Moon’s equator is tipped a few degrees, so we see a little past the poles. Diurnal: we watch from the sides of a spinning Earth, not from its centre.

seeItLive.label: Look for the Moon’s small nod

question: Why does moonrise get later each night?
shortAnswer: The Moon moves east along its orbit while Earth turns. Earth has to spin extra — about 50 minutes — to bring the Moon back to the same place on your sky. That extra is why moonrise (and moonset) slip later day by day.
title: Why Does Moonrise Get Later Each Night?
description: Moonrise is about 50 minutes later each night because Earth must turn extra to catch a Moon that has moved east.
graphicCaption: After one Earth turn the Moon has advanced. The ground must turn farther to find it again.
graphicAlt: Earth turning under a Moon that has moved east along its orbit.

sections.heading: The same 50 minutes as the month
body: A synodic month is about 29.5 days. Spread that extra lap around the sky over 24 hours and you get roughly 50 minutes. The delay is not a separate mystery. It is the month, counted per night.

You can measure it yourself with nothing but your town’s moonrise table: read off a week of moonrise times and take the differences. The gap is not constant — some nights it is 20 minutes, some nights 70 — and that spread is real, not an error in the table.

sections.heading: Why the delay is not always 50 minutes
body: Fifty minutes is the average. The Moon’s path is tilted against your horizon by an angle that changes through the month and the year, and when the path meets the horizon at a shallow angle, the Moon’s nightly step eastward barely delays its rising. Around the September full moon at mid-northern latitudes the delay shrinks to its smallest — several evenings in a row of bright moonrise near sunset. Farmers noticed that long before anyone explained it: it is the harvest moon.

sections.heading: The Sun does it too, invisibly
body: Sunrise also slips against the stars — the Sun drifts about one degree east per day, which is why the stars rise four minutes earlier each night. The Moon’s slip is just thirteen times bigger and easier to notice, because the Moon moves thirteen times faster around the sky. The two slips are the same phenomenon: rise times follow whatever the body does against the turning sky.

seeItLive.label: Compare moonrise times night to night

question: Why isn’t there an eclipse every month?
shortAnswer: The Moon’s path around Earth is tipped about 5° to Earth’s path around the Sun. Most months the full Moon rides above or below Earth’s shadow, and the new Moon rides above or below the Sun. An eclipse needs the Moon at a crossing, not just at a phase.
title: Why Isn’t There an Eclipse Every Month?
description: No monthly eclipse because the Moon’s orbit is tipped about 5°. Full moon usually misses Earth’s shadow.
graphicCaption: Earth’s shadow is a real cone past the Moon’s orbit. A 5° tip is enough for the full Moon to miss that cone most months. The drawing of the tip is exaggerated so you can see it.
graphicAlt: Moon orbit tipped relative to the Sun–Earth line, missing the shadow cone.

sections.heading: Phase is not position on the tilt
body: Full moon means the Moon is opposite the Sun as seen from Earth. It does not mean the three bodies are in a straight line in space. The extra dimension is the 5° tip. Only when a full or new moon happens near a node — a crossing of the two planes — do you get an eclipse.

sections.heading: Why this site’s orrery does not draw the shadow
body: A top-down Sun–Earth–Moon picture flattens the 5°. If it also drew Earth’s umbra as a geometric cone in that plane, the full Moon would sit in the shadow every month and the picture would teach the wrong eclipse. The Earth–Sun–Moon orbit simulator says so, and this page is the reason.

seeItLive.label: See why the shadow is left undrawn

question: How does an orbit change?
shortAnswer: The shape changes, not just the speed. Slow a planet at one point and it drops onto a longer ellipse that swings closer in and climbs back out. Speed it up and the far side lifts away. It does not spiral into the Sun unless almost all of the sideways speed is gone.
title: What Happens When You Change an Orbit?
description: A change in speed is a change in orbit shape. Slow down and the far side drops in; speed up and it lifts. Spiraling into the Sun takes almost all of the sideways motion.
graphicCaption: Take speed away at one point and the far side of the path drops toward the Sun. The planet still comes back through the point where you changed it.
graphicAlt: An elongated ellipse around the Sun, with a planet marked at the point where its speed was changed.

sections.heading: A slider is a thought experiment
body: Nothing in space grabs a planet and changes its speed by hand. What space does is push very gently for a very long time: tides, another planet’s tug, a rare impact. Every one of those shows up the same way — as a different-shaped orbit, not as a faster or slower planet going the same path.
To actually hit the Sun from Earth’s distance you would have to shed almost all of the sideways speed. Anything left is enough to miss.

sections.heading: What can really change an orbit
body: Tides towing the Moon outward a few centimetres a year. Drag on anything low enough to touch an atmosphere. Repeated tugs at a simple period ratio — the gaps in the asteroid belt. An impact, which changes an orbit all at once but only by the momentum it delivers. On the scale of a planet, that last one is disappointing: mass for mass it is much better at changing spin than orbit.

seeItLive.label: Slow a planet and watch the ellipse

question: What is the asteroid belt?
shortAnswer: A ring of leftover rock between Mars and Jupiter. It is not the wreckage of a planet. Jupiter’s gravity never let the rubble gather into one world. The dark gaps in it are resonances — the same tug, at the same point, over and over.
title: What Is the Asteroid Belt?
description: The asteroid belt is leftover rubble between Mars and Jupiter. Jupiter’s gravity kept it from becoming a planet, and carved the gaps inside it.
graphicCaption: The belt sits between Mars and Jupiter. Each rock orbits for the same reason a planet does: it is falling toward the Sun and missing.
graphicAlt: Orbits around the Sun with a band of small bodies between an inner planet and a large outer planet.

sections.heading: Rubble that never became a world
body: The belt’s total mass is about 3% of the Moon’s. Ceres, the largest body in it, is itself a dwarf planet. Switch the belt on in the solar system simulator and you are looking at leftover building material, not a destroyed planet.

sections.heading: The gaps are Jupiter’s doing
body: An asteroid whose year is a simple fraction of Jupiter’s gets the same tug at the same point of its orbit, over and over, until it is pushed out. Those empty lanes are the Kirkwood gaps. The same gravity that kept the belt from becoming a planet is still editing it.

seeItLive.label: Switch the belt on

question: Why are the planets drawn so close together?
shortAnswer: Because the real solar system will not fit on a screen. Neptune is about 78 times farther from the Sun than Mercury. Drawn honestly at one scale, the inner four sit in the innermost tenth of the picture. This simulator climbs a zoom ladder so something is always legible, and it tells you what is compressed.
ledeHtml: Because the real solar system will not fit on a screen. Neptune is about 78 times farther from the Sun than Mercury. Drawn honestly at one scale, the inner four sit in the innermost tenth of the picture. The solar system simulator climbs a zoom ladder so something is always legible, and it tells you what is compressed.
title: Why Are the Planets Drawn So Close?
description: Solar system pictures compress distance so the planets fit. Orbits are to scale within each zoom; the planet dots cannot be, or they would be smaller than a pixel.
graphicCaption: A picture that shows all eight planets at once cannot also show their true sizes. The orbits in each zoom are honest; the dots are sized to be seen.
graphicAlt: Nested planetary orbits around the Sun, with the inner planets clustered near the centre.

sections.heading: What you can trust in the picture
body: The orbits are to scale within one zoom level. Mercury really does lap everyone. Neptune really does barely move in a lifetime. The planet dots are not measurements: at the Saturn view, Jupiter would be a few thousandths of a pixel across. The one exception is the Earth and Moon view, which is to scale in both size and distance at once.

sections.heading: Why a smooth zoom fails
body: Out to Mars the outermost orbit is only tens of times the innermost, and everything is separable. Out to Neptune the ratio is hundreds to one. A smooth zoom spends most of its travel in frames where nothing is legible. Each rung of the ladder is a view where something can be read.

seeItLive.label: Climb the zoom ladder

question: Why is Mars red?
shortAnswer: The dust is rust. Iron in Martian rock has oxidised, and that red-brown powder is blown across the whole planet, so even the sky looks butterscotch. The rocks underneath can be darker; the colour you see from Earth is a planet wearing its rust.
ledeHtml: The dust is rust. Iron in Martian rock has oxidised, and that red-brown powder is blown across the whole planet, so even the sky looks butterscotch. The rocks underneath can be darker; the colour you see from Earth is a planet wearing its rust. Open Mars and its moons to look at the globe.
title: Why Is Mars Red?
description: Mars is red because iron in its dust has rusted. The whole planet is coated in that powder, which is why it looks rust-coloured from Earth.
graphicCaption: Mars drawn from its real features. The rust is in the dust that coats the disc, not a paint job on the rock.
graphicAlt: Mars as a globe, butterscotch with darker patches.

sections.heading: Rust, then wind
body: Early Mars had water and a thicker air. Iron in the rock rusted — the same chemistry that turns a bicycle orange, just much slower and across a whole world. When the water went, the rust stayed as dust.
Mars’s air is thin, but it is enough to lift that dust. Storms can wrap the planet. What you see through a telescope is not bare rock. It is a coat of iron oxide, grain by grain.

sections.heading: Not every rock is red
body: Rovers have found grey-blue rock under the dust, and dark volcanic plains that only look red when the powder sits on them. The colour is a surface story. The planet underneath is a mix, like Earth, just drier and rustier on top.

seeItLive.label: Turn the globe of Mars

question: Why does Triton orbit Neptune backwards?
shortAnswer: Most moons travel the same way their planet spins, because they formed from the same spinning disc. Triton goes the other way, so it did not form next to Neptune. It was captured, almost certainly from the Kuiper belt.
ledeHtml: Most moons travel the same way their planet spins, because they formed from the same spinning disc. Triton goes the other way, so it did not form next to Neptune. It was captured, almost certainly from the Kuiper belt. On Neptune’s moons it is the one that runs backwards.
title: Why Does Triton Orbit Backwards?
description: Triton orbits Neptune the wrong way, so it was captured — almost certainly from the Kuiper belt — rather than born beside the planet.
graphicCaption: Neptune with Triton going the opposite way to the planet’s spin. A moon born in the same disc would not do that.
graphicAlt: Neptune as a globe. Its large moon Triton orbits backwards.

sections.heading: Backwards means captured
body: If a moon forms beside its planet, it inherits the spin of the disc. Clockwise with clockwise, or the other way around — but matching. Triton does not match. That is the giveaway: it arrived later.
The favoured picture is that Triton was one of a pair, like Pluto and Charon. Neptune grabbed one and flung the other away. The leftover is bound, and going the wrong way.

sections.heading: It is spiralling in
body: A backward orbit is also a decaying one. Tides are dragging Triton inward. In some billions of years it will cross Neptune’s Roche limit and break into a ring — unless it hits first. Either way, the system we see is not finished.

seeItLive.label: Watch Triton go the other way

question: Why does Saturn have so many moons?
shortAnswer: Saturn holds the largest confirmed-moon count of any planet, and it keeps climbing as surveys find smaller ones. It is the second-heaviest planet, so an enormous region around it is one where a small icy body stays with Saturn instead of orbiting the Sun. A few large moons formed there; most of the crowd was captured later.
ledeHtml: Gravity’s reach grows with mass. Jupiter and Saturn are the two heaviest planets, so a huge volume of space around each one is a place where a small body stays with the planet instead of orbiting the Sun on its own. Some of those moons formed there. Many more were captured. See Jupiter’s moons and Saturn’s moons.
title: Why Does Saturn Have So Many Moons?
description: Saturn has the most confirmed moons of any planet: a huge gravitational reach, one giant formed moon (Titan), a captured icy crowd — and rings that are not moons.
graphicCaption: Saturn, rings and all. The rings sit inside the region where a moon would be torn apart. The moons sit outside it.
graphicAlt: Saturn as a globe with its ring system.

sections.heading: One giant, then a crowd
body: Titan is the moon that formed beside Saturn the way planets formed beside the Sun, and it holds almost all the mass that orbits the planet — a world bigger than Mercury, with weather and rivers of methane. After Titan come a handful of mid-sized icy moons, and then the census dissolves into hundreds of captured ice-rocks a few kilometres across, on long, tilted, often backwards orbits.

That is why the count keeps changing: the big moons were all found long ago, and what survey telescopes keep adding is the small captured crowd at the bottom of the list. “How many moons does Saturn have” is a census question, not a fixed fact — the honest answer always carries a date.

sections.heading: The rings are not failed moons on the list
body: Inside a certain distance of Saturn, its gravity stretches an orbiting body harder than the body’s own gravity can hold it together — so close in, there can be rings but no large moon. Saturn’s rings live inside that line. Right at its edge sit tiny shepherd moons, herding the ring edges sharp; they are on the moon list, while the countless ring particles they herd are not.

sections.heading: Why the rocky planets keep almost none
body: Earth has one large moon from a giant impact. Mars has two tiny ones. Mercury and Venus have none. Close to the Sun the region where a planet’s gravity beats the Sun’s is small, so there is little room to keep a captured body, and less leftover ice to build one. Mass and distance both decide the guest list — Saturn is heavy and far, so its list is the longest. Jupiter’s answer is the same physics with even more mass behind it.

seeItLive.label: Saturn’s moons
Jupiter’s moons

question: Why do planets have moons, and how are they made?
shortAnswer: Three ways, and you can tell them apart. Some moons form from the same disc as their planet. Some form from the debris of a giant impact. Some are captured — they were going past and got stuck. Triton’s backward orbit is the capture giveaway. Earth’s Moon is the impact story.
ledeHtml: Three ways, and you can tell them apart. Some moons form from the same disc as their planet. Some form from the debris of a giant impact. Some are captured — they were going past and got stuck. Triton’s backward orbit on Neptune is the capture giveaway. Earth’s Moon on the Earth and Moon view is the impact story.
title: Why Do Planets Have Moons?
description: Moons form in three ways: from a disc around the planet, from a giant impact, or by capture. The orbit usually tells you which.
graphicCaption: Jupiter’s four large inner moons formed from a disc around the planet. That is one of the three ways. The tiny outer ones were mostly captured later.
graphicAlt: Jupiter as a globe with nested inner moon orbits.

sections.heading: Disc, smash, or grab
body: A disc moon sits on a tidy, forward, nearly circular orbit near the equator — Io, Europa, Titan. An impact moon can be huge compared with its planet: our Moon is a quarter of Earth’s width; Charon is half of Pluto’s. A captured moon often comes in on a tilted or backward path, like Triton.
The same falling-and-missing that keeps a planet beside the Sun keeps a moon beside a planet. More mass, a larger volume of space where “beside the planet” wins.

sections.heading: Earth’s Moon is the odd one in the inner system
body: A Mars-sized body hit the young Earth. Debris went into orbit and became the Moon. That much is broadly agreed. The puzzle is that the Moon’s rocks look almost identical to Earth’s, while most impact models make a moon out of the impactor. Getting a Moon that looks like Earth’s mantle out of a collision with something else is still an unsolved modelling problem.

seeItLive.label: A disc of moons around Jupiter
Earth and Moon to scale

question: How were the planets formed?
shortAnswer: From a spinning disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Dust stuck, then pebbles, then worlds. Close in it was too warm for ice, so the inner four stayed small and rocky. Farther out, ice and gas stayed put, gravity grabbed hydrogen, and the giants grew huge.
ledeHtml: From a spinning disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Dust stuck, then pebbles, then worlds. Close in it was too warm for ice, so the inner four stayed small and rocky. Farther out, ice and gas stayed put, gravity grabbed hydrogen, and the giants grew huge. The solar system simulator is that disc, later: everything still going the same way, in nearly the same plane.
title: How Were the Planets Formed?
description: The planets grew from a spinning disc around the young Sun. Inside the snow line they stayed rocky; outside it they could grab ice and gas and become giants.
graphicCaption: One disc, one direction. That is why the planets still orbit the same way, in nearly the same plane, billions of years later.
graphicAlt: Planets on nested orbits around the Sun, all travelling the same way.

sections.heading: A disc, then worlds
body: The young Sun was surrounded by a flat cloud of gas and dust, spinning. Grains stuck. Pebbles stuck. After a few million years there were bodies the size of towns, then of moons, then of planets. Leftover gas either got blown out or got pulled onto the biggest worlds.

You can still see the disc in the finished system: almost everything goes the same way, and almost everything sits in the same thin plane. The exceptions — Venus spinning backwards, Uranus on its side, Triton going the wrong way — each need an extra event.

sections.heading: They did not finish where they sit
body: Models in which the giant planets drifted inward and back out — dragging small bodies, emptying part of the asteroid belt, scattering the Kuiper belt — reproduce a great deal of what we see. Which version happened, and when, is not agreed. The zoom ladder shows where they are now, not the road they took.

seeItLive.label: The finished disc, as it is today

question: Why doesn’t Earth have a ring?
shortAnswer: A ring is ice or rock that orbits inside a limit where a moon would be pulled apart. Earth could wear one if a moon broke up that close. Our Moon is too far out and too well stuck together. Saturn’s rings are the famous leftover — ice that never quite made a moon, or a moon that came too close.
ledeHtml: A ring is ice or rock that orbits inside a limit where a moon would be pulled apart. Earth could wear one if a moon broke up that close. Our Moon is too far out and too well stuck together. Saturn’s rings on Saturn and its moons are the famous leftover — ice that never quite made a moon, or a moon that came too close.
title: Why Doesn’t Earth Have a Ring?
description: Earth has no ring because its Moon sits well outside the distance where a moon would be torn into one. Saturn’s rings live inside that limit.
graphicCaption: Saturn’s rings sit inside the region where a moon would be torn apart. Outside that line, moons survive. Earth’s Moon is far outside Earth’s equivalent line.
graphicAlt: Saturn as a globe with its broad ring system.

sections.heading: The Roche limit
body: Too close to a planet, tides across a moon are stronger than the moon’s own gravity. The moon comes apart and the pieces spread into a ring. That distance is the Roche limit. Saturn’s bright rings live inside it. Titan lives outside it.

Earth has a Roche limit too, only a few Earth-radii up. Our Moon is about 60 Earth-radii away. It is in no danger of becoming a ring. If something ice-rich wandered in that close, Earth could wear a faint ring for a while — but nothing that size is on that path now.

sections.heading: The giants all have some kind of ring
body: Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have faint dusty rings as well as Saturn’s ice boulders. One idea is that a ring is a phase every giant goes through: moons grind down, dust is replaced, the show fades. Saturn’s would then be a bright snapshot of something the others have already finished. Earth never had the leftover ice at the right distance, and its one large moon formed much farther out.

seeItLive.label: Saturn’s rings and moons
Earth and Moon, no ring

question: Why does Pluto, such a small world, have so many moons?
shortAnswer: A giant impact likely made Charon and left a debris disc that became Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra. Charon is half Pluto’s width, so the two of them are a double world — and the four small moons sit in the gravity of the pair, not of a single point.
ledeHtml: A giant impact likely made Charon and left a debris disc that became Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra. Charon is half Pluto’s width, so the two of them are a double world — and the four small moons sit in the gravity of the pair, not of a single point. See them on Pluto and its moons.
title: Why Does Pluto Have So Many Moons?
description: Pluto’s five moons likely come from one giant impact: Charon is the big leftover, and four small moons condensed from the debris.
graphicCaption: Pluto and Charon are a pair. The four small moons orbit both of them. A body this small keeps a crowd because of that one smash, not because it is massive like Jupiter.
graphicAlt: Pluto as a globe.

sections.heading: One smash, five moons
body: Charon is so big that the point Pluto and Charon both orbit sits outside Pluto’s surface. No other named pair in the solar system does that. The four small moons — Styx, Nix, Kerberos, Hydra — go round the pair on tidy, nearly circular paths, which is what you expect from leftover debris after an impact, not from random captures.
Small does not mean moonless. It means the moons, if they exist, probably share one origin story rather than a billion years of capture.

sections.heading: The little four tumble
body: Styx, Nix, Kerberos and Hydra do not keep one face to Pluto. They sit in the gravity of a rotating pair rather than a single point, so their day lengths change in a way that looks random from month to month. New Horizons watched that tumble on one afternoon in 2015. Nobody has been back.

seeItLive.label: Pluto, Charon and the small four

question: Why is Pluto a dwarf planet and not a planet?
shortAnswer: A planet has to clear its neighbourhood. Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with a great many other bodies, one of them — Eris — more massive than Pluto. The world itself did not get smaller in 2006. The rule about the neighbourhood did.
ledeHtml: A planet has to clear its neighbourhood. Pluto shares the Kuiper belt with a great many other bodies, one of them — Eris — more massive than Pluto. The world itself did not get smaller in 2006. The rule about the neighbourhood did. Pluto and its moons is still a place: ice mountains, a nitrogen glacier, five moons.
title: Why Is Pluto a Dwarf Planet?
description: Pluto is a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood. It shares the Kuiper belt with many other worlds, including Eris.
graphicCaption: The label is about the neighbourhood, not the world. Pluto is still 2,377 km across, with weather, ice mountains and a large companion.
graphicAlt: Pluto as a globe.

sections.heading: Three tests, and Pluto fails the third
body: In 2006 the IAU asked three things of a planet: it orbits the Sun, it is round because of its own gravity, and it has cleared the other things on its path. Pluto does the first two. It fails the third. The Kuiper belt is full of leftover worlds on similar orbits. Ceres, in the asteroid belt, fails the same test.
Calling it a dwarf planet is a statement about the region, not an insult to the ice. New Horizons found mountains, a heart-shaped glacier with no craters on it, and a blue haze in dozens of layers.

sections.heading: Why the rule exists
body: If roundness alone made a planet, the solar system would have dozens, and more every time a telescope found another round Kuiper belt object. The neighbourhood test keeps “planet” for the eight that dominate their paths. It is a census rule. It does not change what Pluto is made of, or that Charon makes it a double world.

seeItLive.label: Pluto as a world
Where it sits in the list

question: Do other planets have seasons?
shortAnswer: Yes, if they tilt. Seasons come from a lean, not from being closer to the Sun. Mars tilts about 25°, like Earth, so it has seasons — just longer, because its year is longer. Uranus tilts 98°, so each pole sits in sunlight for 42 years and then in darkness for 42. Jupiter barely tilts, so its seasons are weak.
ledeHtml: Yes, if they tilt. Seasons come from a lean, not from being closer to the Sun. Mars tilts about 25°, like Earth, so it has seasons — just longer, because its year is longer. Uranus tilts 98°, so each pole sits in sunlight for 42 years and then in darkness for 42. See the lean on Uranus, and Earth’s own year on the Earth–Sun–Moon orbit simulator.
title: Do Other Planets Have Seasons?
description: Seasons come from axial tilt. Mars has Earth-like seasons on a longer year. Uranus, tipped on its side, gives each pole 42 years of day then 42 of night.
graphicCaption: Uranus lies on its side. That 98° tilt is the most extreme season in the solar system: each pole, 42 years of sun, then 42 years of night.
graphicAlt: Uranus as a globe, axis nearly in the plane of its orbit.

sections.heading: Tilt, not distance
body: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, which is northern winter. Distance is the wrong story. The axis leans, so for half the year the north end points toward the Sun and for the other half it points away. Any planet with a lean gets a version of that.

Mars’s year is about 687 Earth days, so each season lasts about twice as long as ours. Its ice caps grow and shrink. Dust storms prefer the warmer half. Uranus rolls: one pole then the other takes a 42-year polar day.

sections.heading: Jupiter almost does not bother
body: Jupiter’s tilt is only about 3°. The Sun’s height in its sky barely changes over a year, so there is little seasonal contrast. Neptune tilts about 28°, similar to Earth, but one Neptune year is 165 of ours — a “season” there is measured in decades. The rule is the same on every world: the lean sets the pattern, the year sets the clock.

seeItLive.label: Uranus on its side
Earth’s tilt through a year

question: Why aren’t the inner planets gas giants?
shortAnswer: Close to the Sun it was too warm for ice and light gas to stick. The inner four could only build from rock and metal, so they stayed small. Past a line called the snow line, ice piled on, gravity grabbed hydrogen and helium, and the giants grew huge.
ledeHtml: Close to the Sun it was too warm for ice and light gas to stick. The inner four could only build from rock and metal, so they stayed small. Past a line called the snow line, ice piled on, gravity grabbed hydrogen and helium, and the giants grew huge. The solar system simulator still shows that split: four small inner worlds, then a jump.
title: Why Aren’t the Inner Planets Gas Giants?
description: The inner planets are rocky because they formed inside the snow line, where ice and gas could not stick. The giants formed farther out, where they could.
graphicCaption: Inside the snow line: rock. Outside it: ice and gas, and the mass to hold them. The jump between Mars and Jupiter is that line, later.
graphicAlt: Nested orbits around the Sun, inner planets close in, giants farther out.

sections.heading: A temperature line in the disc
body: In the disc around the young Sun, water was vapour close in and ice farther out. Rock could stick either side of that line. Ice could not stick inside it. So the inner four grew from rock and metal only, and never got massive enough to hold a thick envelope of hydrogen.

Outside the line, ice was extra building material. More mass, more gravity, and those worlds could pull in the leftover gas before the Sun blew it away. Jupiter and Saturn won that race. Uranus and Neptune got there later and grabbed less gas, which is why they are ice giants rather than hydrogen balls.

sections.heading: The missing super-Earth
body: Planets between the size of Earth and Neptune are the commonest kind found around other stars, and our system does not have one. There is a gap between Earth and Neptune where most systems put their most typical planet. Jupiter’s early drift is the usual explanation. It is a model, not a photograph of the past.

seeItLive.label: Four small, then the jump to Jupiter

question: Why didn’t the asteroid belt turn into a planet?
shortAnswer: There was never enough rock, and Jupiter never let it gather. Everything in the belt together is about 3% of the Moon’s mass. Collisions smashed rather than stuck, because Jupiter’s gravity stirred the region. It is leftover building material, not a planet that broke.
ledeHtml: There was never enough rock, and Jupiter never let it gather. Everything in the belt together is about 3% of the Moon’s mass. Collisions smashed rather than stuck, because Jupiter’s gravity stirred the region. It is leftover building material, not a planet that broke. Switch it on in the asteroid belt view.
title: Why Didn’t the Asteroid Belt Become a Planet?
description: The asteroid belt never became a planet: too little mass, and Jupiter’s gravity made collisions destructive instead of constructive.
graphicCaption: A ring of leftovers between Mars and Jupiter. Not the wreckage of a world — a world that was never allowed to finish.
graphicAlt: Orbits around the Sun with a band of small bodies between Mars and Jupiter.

sections.heading: Not enough, and too stirred
body: Add up every asteroid and you still do not have a planet. Ceres, the largest, is itself a dwarf planet and only about a third of the belt’s mass. A planet needs material and quiet. The belt had little of the first and none of the second.
Jupiter is next door. Its tugs sped things up and changed their paths, so when two bodies met they tended to shatter instead of stick. The same gravity still carves empty lanes in the belt today.

sections.heading: The belt used to be heavier
body: Models in which the giant planets migrated throw most of the original belt away and mix in bodies from elsewhere. That would explain why the belt holds both dry inner-system rock and water-rich outer-system material. How much was thrown, and when, is not settled. What is left is the quiet remnant.

seeItLive.label: Switch the belt on

question: Do asteroids in the asteroid belt collide?
shortAnswer: Yes, but rarely. Typical named bodies sit about a million kilometres apart, so the belt is empty, not a pinball table. When two do hit, they make a family of fragments on similar orbits. Spacecraft fly through without dodging.
ledeHtml: Yes, but rarely. Typical named bodies sit about a million kilometres apart, so the belt is empty, not a pinball table. When two do hit, they make a family of fragments on similar orbits. Spacecraft fly through without dodging. The asteroid belt view is honest about how spread out they are.
title: Do Asteroids in the Asteroid Belt Collide?
description: Asteroids do collide, but the belt is so spread out that hits are rare. Films pack it; the real gap between named bodies is about a million kilometres.
graphicCaption: Every spacecraft sent to the outer solar system has flown through the belt without a course change for debris. That is how empty it is.
graphicAlt: A sparse band of small bodies between Mars and Jupiter.

sections.heading: Empty, with occasional smash-ups
body: Films pack the belt so the hero has to dodge. The real thing is the opposite. The typical gap between objects large enough to name is on the order of a million kilometres. You could sit in a ship for a long time and see nothing.

Over millions of years, some of them do meet. A hit can make a family: fragments that still share a similar orbit, which is how we know a collision happened. Most of the belt, most of the time, just goes around.

sections.heading: Jupiter still picks the fights
body: Resonances with Jupiter pump some asteroids onto crossing paths, which is when a collision — or a path toward Earth — becomes more likely. The Kirkwood gaps are those pumped lanes, emptied. The belt is not a closed box. It leaks, slowly, because Jupiter never stopped stirring.

seeItLive.label: See how spread out the belt is

question: What is a time zone?
shortAnswer: A political stripe painted on a rotating ball. Noon is where the Sun is overhead. A zone is an argument about how far from that line a country is willing to sit, so clocks in that stripe all say the same hour.
ledeHtml: A political stripe painted on a rotating ball. Noon is where the Sun is overhead. A zone is an argument about how far from that line a country is willing to sit, so clocks in that stripe all say the same hour. See it on the world clock and the day/night map.
title: What Is a Time Zone?
description: A time zone is a political stripe on a rotating Earth. Noon is where the Sun is overhead; the zone is how far from that a country is willing to sit.
graphicCaption: The Sun is overhead along one meridian. Everything east of it is already later. The stripes we call zones are cut into that.
graphicAlt: Day and night world map, the lit half showing where it is day right now.

sections.heading: Noon is a place
body: If Earth had one clock, noon would travel west around the planet every day and the date would never know where to jump. Zones freeze a whole stripe at one hour so neighbours can agree.
The stripes are not honest meridians. China is one zone. India is a half-hour off everyone. Those are political choices, visible on the world clock.

sections.heading: The map is the reason
body: The day/night map is why zones exist: the terminator is a moving line, and every zone is a bet about how far from the overhead Sun a country will let its clocks sit.

seeItLive.label: Who is awake right now
The Sun overhead, as a place

question: What is UTC?
shortAnswer: Coordinated Universal Time — the one clock the rest are offsets from. It tracks atomic time, steered to stay close to the Earth’s spin. Every zone on this site is written as hours ahead of or behind UTC.
title: What Is UTC?
description: UTC is the one clock every time zone is an offset from. This site computes in UTC, then shows you your own zone.
graphicCaption: No picture needed: UTC is an agreement, not a place. The 0 on every offset.
graphicAlt: UTC is the zero offset every time zone is counted from.

sections.heading: The zero the others are counted from
body: New York is UTC−5 in winter, UTC−4 in summer. Tokyo is UTC+9 all year. The number is the difference from this one clock.
This site solves the sky in UTC, then writes the result in your zone. That is why a full moon is one instant worldwide and a different clock reading in each city.

sections.heading: Atomic time, steered to Earth
body: UTC is kept by atomic clocks and occasionally a leap second is added so it does not drift far from the Earth’s actual spin. The difference is tiny. For anything on this site, UTC is the honest now.

seeItLive.label: Every zone as an offset from UTC

question: What is daylight saving time?
shortAnswer: A twice-a-year decision to shift the clock one hour so evening daylight lasts longer in summer. Not every place does it. When they do, the offset from UTC changes, and so does the sunrise time on the clock — not the sunrise in the sky.
ledeHtml: A twice-a-year decision to shift the clock one hour so evening daylight lasts longer in summer. Not every place does it. When they do, the offset from UTC changes, and so does the sunrise time on the clock — not the sunrise in the sky. The sunrise pages follow the zone’s real rules.
title: What Is Daylight Saving Time?
description: Daylight saving time shifts the clock one hour. The Sun does not move. Sunrise on the clock changes; sunrise in the sky does not.
graphicCaption: The sky does not spring forward. The labels on the clock do.
graphicAlt: Daylight saving time is a clock shift, not a change in the Sun.

sections.heading: The sky does not change
body: On the spring-forward night, 2:00 a.m. becomes 3:00 a.m. You lose an hour of sleep. The Sun still rises when the Earth has turned far enough. Only the number on the clock jumped.
Arizona (mostly) and Hawaii do not do this. Most of Europe does. That is why a world clock has to know the rules, not just a fixed offset.

sections.heading: Why the clock, not the Sun
body: The original pitch was to move an hour of daylight from the morning, when fewer people are out, to the evening. Whether it saves energy is argued. What it definitely does is change every offset from UTC for a few months, which is why a sunrise table that ignored DST would be an hour wrong all summer.

seeItLive.label: Sunrise in a zone that actually shifts

question: What is a solar day?
shortAnswer: Sunrise to sunrise — the day you actually live. On Earth that averages 24 hours. A full spin relative to the stars is about 4 minutes shorter, because Earth also moved along its orbit and has to turn a little extra to face the Sun again.
title: What Is a Solar Day?
description: A solar day is sunrise to sunrise. On Earth it averages 24 hours, a few minutes longer than one full spin relative to the stars.
graphicCaption: Earth has to turn a little extra each day to catch the Sun, because it also moved along its orbit.
graphicAlt: A solar day is sunrise to sunrise, a few minutes longer than one spin.

sections.heading: The day the Sun makes
body: If you watch a sundial, noon is when the shadow is shortest. That interval — noon to noon — is a solar day. We split it into 24 hours.
Mars does this too: a Martian solar day (a sol) is about 24 hours 40 minutes. The planets page lists the spin; this is the other number.

sections.heading: Why it is not exactly 24 hours every day
body: Earth’s orbit is a slight ellipse and its axis is tilted, so the true solar day wanders by a quarter-hour over the year. That wander is the equation of time. Clocks ignore it and run a mean 24 hours.

seeItLive.label: Noon as a shadow, for your town

question: What is a sidereal day?
shortAnswer: One full turn relative to the stars, not the Sun. On Earth that is 23 hours 56 minutes. A star rises about four minutes earlier each night because of that difference — which is the orbit showing up in the clock.
title: What Is a Sidereal Day?
description: A sidereal day is one full turn relative to the stars: 23 hours 56 minutes on Earth. That is why a star rises four minutes earlier each night.
graphicCaption: The planets page lists this number as “one full turn.” It is the spin, not sunrise to sunrise.
graphicAlt: A sidereal day is one spin relative to the stars.

sections.heading: Why stars rise earlier
body: Face a star at 9 p.m. Tomorrow the same star is up at 8:56 p.m. Earth spun once relative to the stars in 23 h 56 m, then kept turning a little more to face the Sun. That extra is why the night sky shifts through the year.

sections.heading: The number on the planets page
body: When the planets page says Earth’s day is 23.9 hours, it means this: one full turn. Mars 24.6 hours is the same kind of number. Sunrise to sunrise is the solar day, a few minutes longer.

seeItLive.label: One full turn, for every world

question: What is a leap year?
shortAnswer: A year with 29 February. The Earth takes about 365.242 days to go around the Sun, so a 365-day calendar drifts. Adding a day most years that divide by 4 — but not most centuries — keeps the seasons from walking off the months.
ledeHtml: A year with 29 February. The Earth takes about 365.242 days to go around the Sun, so a 365-day calendar drifts. Adding a day most years that divide by 4 — but not most centuries — keeps the seasons from walking off the months. There is a leap-year lesson that runs this as a class.
title: What Is a Leap Year?
description: A leap year adds 29 February because Earth takes about 365.242 days to orbit the Sun. The extra day keeps the calendar lined up with the seasons.
graphicCaption: The extra day is a correction for a year that is not a whole number of days.
graphicAlt: A leap year adds one day because Earth’s year is not a whole number of days.

sections.heading: The leftover quarter-day
body: If every year were 365 days, the calendar would lose about a quarter-day a year — a day every four years, a month every 120, a season every 700. Spring would slide into December.
Most years that divide by 4 get 29 February. 1900 did not. 2000 did. That is the century rule, and it is why the calendar still matches the seasons.

sections.heading: The year is not 365.25 either
body: 365.2422, more nearly. The Gregorian skip-three-centuries-in-four rule approximates that. The remaining error is about a day in a few thousand years. Good enough that the seasons stay put on the months we named for them.

seeItLive.label: The orbit whose stray quarter-day the leap year absorbs

question: What is the International Date Line?
shortAnswer: The seam where the calendar jumps a day. Noon travels west around a round Earth forever, so somewhere the date has to tear. We cut the seam in the Pacific, as far from most people as we could, and kink it around islands that did not want to be split.
ledeHtml: The seam where the calendar jumps a day. Noon travels west around a round Earth forever, so somewhere the date has to tear. We cut the seam in the Pacific, as far from most people as we could, and kink it around islands that did not want to be split. On the world clock, Auckland and Honolulu are often on two different dates at the same moment.
title: What Is the International Date Line?
description: The International Date Line is the seam where the calendar jumps a day, cut through the Pacific so noon can travel west around a round Earth forever.
graphicCaption: Same moment, two dates. The line is not magic. It is the cut you are forced to make on a round Earth with a calendar.
graphicAlt: A world map. Somewhere on it the calendar has to jump a day.

sections.heading: The forced cut
body: If you fly west around the world, you keep setting your watch back. When you get home, a day has gone missing unless you add one somewhere. That somewhere is this line.
It kinks around Kiribati, around eastern Russia, around a few islands that picked a side. The kinks are politics. The need for a seam is geometry.

sections.heading: Two cities, two dates
body: Open the world clock and find a pair — Auckland and Honolulu usually work. Same instant, different date. There is no moment when the whole world shares one calendar day.

seeItLive.label: Find two cities on two dates

question: What is the equation of time?
shortAnswer: The difference between clock noon and sundial noon. The Earth’s orbit is a slight ellipse and its axis is tilted, so the true solar day wanders by up to about 16 minutes through the year. Clocks run a mean 24 hours and ignore it.
title: What Is the Equation of Time?
description: The equation of time is the difference between clock noon and sundial noon, up to about 16 minutes, caused by Earth’s elliptical orbit and tilt.
graphicCaption: A sundial and a clock disagree by up to 16 minutes, and they disagree on a schedule.
graphicAlt: Clock noon and sundial noon are not the same time of day.

sections.heading: Why a sundial is 'wrong'
body: In November a sundial can run a quarter-hour fast. In February it can run slow. The clock is the one that is smoothed. The sundial is following the real Sun.
Two effects add up: the orbit is not a circle, so Earth speeds up and slows down, and the axis is tilted, so the Sun’s path along the equator is not even. Together they are this equation.

sections.heading: The analemma
body: Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and the spots make a figure-8. That shape is the equation of time plotted against the Sun’s changing height. It is the tilt and the ellipse, drawn in the sky.

seeItLive.label: Sunrise and noon for your town

question: What is the 24-hour clock?
shortAnswer: The clock that does not hide the afternoon. 07:00 is morning; 19:00 is evening. Science, airlines, hospitals and most of the world use it because 7:00 on a 12-hour clock throws away the answer to breakfast or dinner.
ledeHtml: The clock that does not hide the afternoon. 07:00 is morning; 19:00 is evening. Science, airlines, hospitals and most of the world use it because 7:00 on a 12-hour clock throws away the answer to breakfast or dinner. Convert any time on the 12- and 24-hour converter.
title: What Is the 24-Hour Clock?
description: The 24-hour clock numbers the whole day 00:00 to 23:59, so 19:00 cannot be confused with 7:00 in the morning.
graphicCaption: One trip around the clock face is one day, not half of one.
graphicAlt: The 24-hour clock numbers the whole day from 00:00 to 23:59.

sections.heading: Who cannot afford the ambiguity
body: Write 7:00 on a board and ask: breakfast or dinner? You cannot know. Pilots, doctors, train drivers, armies, scientists: everyone whose mistake would matter uses the clock that keeps the afternoon.
This site’s timers and alarms can show either. The converter is the lesson: have a class write their day in 24-hour time and check it.

sections.heading: Midnight is 00:00, not 24:00
body: 24:00 is sometimes written for the end of a day, but civil time starts the new day at 00:00. UTC uses 00:00. So does this site.

seeItLive.label: Convert a time

question: How do you calculate military time?
shortAnswer: Morning hours keep their number: 9:00 AM is 0900. From 1:00 PM onward, add 12 to the hour: 1:00 PM becomes 1300, 9:30 PM becomes 2130. Midnight is 0000. To convert back, subtract 12 from any hour of 13 or higher. The minutes never change — only the hour and the AM/PM label.
ledeHtml: Two rules do all of it. In the morning, the hour keeps its number: 9:00 AM is 0900 — “oh-nine-hundred.” From 1:00 PM on, add 12 to the hour: 1:00 PM is 1300, 6:15 PM is 1815, 9:30 PM is 2130. Coming back the other way, subtract 12 from any hour of 13 or more. The minutes never move. Military time is the 24-hour clock with the colon dropped and a zero up front — the same clock with the afternoon un-hidden — and the chart below has every hour already worked out.
title: How Do You Calculate Military Time?
description: Add 12 to any PM hour: 1:00 PM is 1300, 9:30 PM is 2130. Morning hours keep their number, midnight is 0000, and the minutes never change.
graphicCaption: Every hour of the day in both clocks. Find your hour on either side and read across — the minutes carry over unchanged.
graphicAlt: A table of all 24 hours showing each 12-hour clock time beside its 24-hour equivalent.

sections.heading: The two rules, worked through
body: AM hours: write the hour with two digits and put the minutes straight after. 7:05 AM is 0705; 11:59 AM is 1159. The only odd one is the first hour of the day: 12:30 AM is 0030, because the day starts at zero, not at twelve.

PM hours: add 12. So 1:00 PM is 1300, 4:45 PM is 1645, 11:00 PM is 2300. Noon stays 1200 — it is the last hour that keeps its number. Check yourself against the chart above, or type a time into the converter and see whether you agree.

sections.heading: How to say it
body: Whole hours are read as hundreds: 0900 is “oh-nine-hundred,” 1300 is “thirteen-hundred.” With minutes, read the pairs: 2130 is “twenty-one thirty.” Nobody says “o’clock” — the number already says which half of the day it is, which is the point.

sections.heading: Why midnight is 0000 and not 2400
body: A day runs from 0000 to 2359. The moment a clock would read 2400, a new day has begun and it reads 0000 instead. You will occasionally see 2400 on a schedule to mean “the very end of this day” — the same instant as the next day’s 0000, just different bookkeeping.

sections.heading: Who cannot afford the 12-hour clock
body: Write 7:00 on a whiteboard and it could be breakfast or dinner — the 12-hour clock throws that information away and trusts context to rescue you. Pilots, nurses, train crews, soldiers and scientists work where context does not rescue you, so they use the clock that cannot be misread. Aviation and the military go a step further and pin the clock to one shared zone: 0900Z — “Zulu” — means 0900 UTC, the same instant everywhere on Earth.

seeItLive.label: Convert any time, both directions
Every city’s clock, with the 12/24 switch

question: What is a solstice?
shortAnswer: A solstice is a day the Sun reaches the farthest point it ever gets from the equator — {tilt}° north around {juneSolstice}, {tilt}° south around {decSolstice}. For the hemisphere leaning in it is the longest day of the year; for the other, the shortest. The word means “the Sun stands still”: its slow drift north or south stops and turns around.
ledeHtml: A solstice is a day the Sun reaches the farthest point it ever gets from the equator. Around {juneSolstice} it stands straight over the Tropic of Cancer, {tilt}° north — the longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere and the shortest in the southern. Around {decSolstice} it stands over the Tropic of Capricorn and the hemispheres swap. The word is Latin — sol, the Sun, and sistere, to stand still — because the Sun’s drift north or south stops on this day and reverses. That farthest-ever figure, {tilt}°, is Earth’s tilt, and that is no coincidence: a solstice is the tilt, seen from the ground.
title: What Is a Solstice?
description: A solstice is the day the Sun stands farthest from the equator — over a tropic around {juneSolstice} or {decSolstice}: the year's longest and shortest days.
graphicCaption: The June solstice from the side: sunlight meets Earth {tilt}° north of the equator — as far north as the overhead Sun ever gets. Six months later the picture flips south.
graphicAlt: Side view of Earth at the June solstice, with sunlight arriving directly over the Tropic of Cancer.

sections.heading: Longest day, not earliest sunrise
body: The June solstice has the most daylight in the north, but the earliest sunrise lands about a week before it and the latest sunset about a week after. The two ends of the day do not move in step, because clock noon and Sun noon drift apart through the year — the equation of time. The whole pattern is sitting in the 7-day table on your own town’s sun page if you look at the week around the solstice.

sections.heading: What actually stands still
body: Watch where the Sun rises for a few weeks and it slides along the horizon, a little further north each morning through northern spring. At the solstice the slide stops, holds for a few days, and heads back the other way. That is the standing-still the name records — not the Sun pausing in the sky, but the turning point of its year.

sections.heading: At the polar circles it is all or nothing
body: On the June solstice the Sun does not set anywhere inside the Arctic Circle, and does not rise anywhere inside the Antarctic Circle. The polar circles sit at 90° minus {tilt} — the tilt’s other signature. Jump to a solstice on the day/night map and you can see it: the top of the map entirely lit, or entirely dark.

sections.heading: Why the hottest weeks come later
body: The most sunlight is not the most heat. Land and ocean keep warming for as long as each day still delivers more energy than its night sheds, so the temperature peak lags the light peak by several weeks — July and August in the north, January and February in the south. The sea lags hardest of all, which is why beach water is warmest long after the longest day has gone.

seeItLive.label: Jump straight to a solstice on the live map
Your own longest and shortest day, computed for your town

question: What is an equinox?
shortAnswer: An equinox is one of the two days a year the Sun stands directly over the equator — around {marEquinox} and again around {sepEquinox}. Day and night are then close to twelve hours each everywhere on Earth, pole to pole. One equinox starts spring in your hemisphere; the other starts fall.
ledeHtml: An equinox is a day the Sun stands directly over the equator, which happens twice a year — around {marEquinox} and around {sepEquinox}. On those days the day/night line runs through both poles and everywhere on Earth gets close to twelve hours of daylight; the name is Latin for “equal night.” The March equinox begins spring in the northern hemisphere and fall in the southern, and the September one swaps them. Between equinoxes, the overhead Sun is always somewhere on its way from one tropic to the other.
title: What Is an Equinox?
description: An equinox is a day the Sun stands over the equator — around {marEquinox} and {sepEquinox} — and day and night run close to twelve hours each, everywhere on Earth.
graphicCaption: The side view at an equinox: sunlight meets Earth square-on to the equator, and the day/night line runs pole to pole.
graphicAlt: Side view of Earth at an equinox, with sunlight arriving directly over the equator and the terminator passing through both poles.

sections.heading: The one day the map is symmetric
body: Jump to an equinox on the day/night map and the shadow’s edge stands nearly vertical — every latitude cut in half. It is the only date that is true. The poles split the difference most strangely of all: there the Sun rolls along the horizon, taking days to fully rise or fully set. An equinox at the pole is not a day — it is the hinge between a six-month day and a six-month night.

sections.heading: “Equal” is approximate
body: Check your own sunrise table on the equinox and you will find slightly more than twelve hours of daylight. Two honest reasons: sunrise and sunset are counted from the Sun’s top edge rather than its centre, and the air bends the low Sun upward into view, stretching both ends of the day by a few minutes. The date when day and night truly measure equal — the equilux — falls a few days toward the winter side.

sections.heading: Why the date wobbles between the 19th and the 21st
body: The equinox is an instant, not a date — the moment the overhead Sun crosses the equator. A real year of seasons is about a quarter of a day longer than 365 days, so that instant lands about six hours later each calendar year, then jumps back a day when the leap day is inserted. That is the same stray quarter-day the leap year exists to absorb, showing up as a wobbling date.

seeItLive.label: Jump straight to an equinox on the live map
Check your own equinox daylight against twelve hours

question: What is a supermoon?
shortAnswer: A supermoon is a full moon that happens near the Moon’s closest approach to Earth. The orbit is an ellipse, not a circle — the distance swings by about 14% — so some full moons are closer, larger and brighter than others. There is no official cutoff, which is why a supermoon list should show each full moon’s actual distance.
ledeHtml: A supermoon is a full moon that lands near perigee, the closest point of the Moon’s orbit. The orbit is an ellipse: the distance swings between roughly 357,000 and 407,000 km, about 14% end to end, so a full moon at the near end looks a little bigger and meaningfully brighter than one at the far end. “Supermoon” is not an astronomer’s term and has no official definition — which is why the supermoon list on this site names the threshold it uses and prints every full moon’s distance beside it, so you can see the choice being made.
title: What Is a Supermoon?
description: A supermoon is a full moon near the Moon’s closest approach. The orbit’s distance swings about 14%, so the closest full moons run larger and about 30% brighter.
graphicCaption: The Moon on its orbit right now. The drawing’s circle is a simplification — the real orbit is an ellipse, and a supermoon is about where on that ellipse a full moon lands.
graphicAlt: The Moon on its orbit around Earth, with the Sun’s direction setting the phase.

sections.heading: What you would actually notice
body: Side by side, the year’s closest full moon is about 14% wider than its most distant one — a coin next to a very slightly larger coin. From memory, a month apart, you would struggle to call it. Brightness is the real difference: light grows with the area of the disc, so the closest full moons run around 30% brighter than the farthest. And the famous giant moon sitting on the horizon is a different thing entirely — the phase is real, but the horizon-hugeness is an illusion your brain adds at any distance.

sections.heading: A coincidence of two cycles
body: The Moon passes its closest point every single orbit, so a supermoon is not a rare approach — it is a coincidence of timing, full phase and closest approach landing together. The cycle of phases (about 29.5 days) runs slightly longer than the orbit’s own close-far cycle, so the full moon slowly slides around the ellipse, and roughly every fourteen months a run of two or three full moons lands near the close end.

sections.heading: The tides notice more than you do
body: The Moon’s tide-raising grip strengthens faster with closeness than its brightness does. A full moon is already a spring-tide alignment; a full moon at perigee stacks the two, and those “perigean spring tides” run measurably higher — they are the king tides that make coastal news. If flood warnings follow a supermoon by a day or two, that is the same coincidence of cycles, read from the beach.

question: What is a blue moon?
shortAnswer: A blue moon is the second full moon inside one calendar month. Phases repeat about every 29.5 days and most months are 30 or 31 days long, so a full moon on the 1st or 2nd leaves just enough room for another before the month ends. It happens roughly every two to three years — and the Moon does not turn blue.
ledeHtml: A blue moon is the second full moon to fall inside one calendar month. The cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days — a synodic month — and most calendar months are 30 or 31 days, so a full moon on the 1st or 2nd leaves just enough room for a second before the month runs out. That squeeze only works out every two to three years, which is what “once in a blue moon” has come to mean. The Moon itself looks exactly as it always does; the blue-moon list on this site works out every one that is coming.
title: What Is a Blue Moon?
description: A blue moon is the second full moon in one calendar month — possible because phases repeat every 29.5 days and months run 30 or 31. About every two to three years.
graphicCaption: Tonight’s phase. A blue moon looks exactly like any other full moon — the name is about the calendar, not the colour.
graphicAlt: The Moon on its orbit around Earth, showing tonight’s phase.

sections.heading: Why a month can fit two full moons
body: A calendar month is a container built for the Moon’s cycle — the word comes from “moon” — but built slightly too big, rounded up to 30 or 31 days. A container one or two days roomier than the thing it holds will occasionally hold the start of a second one. February is the exception in both directions: at 28 or 29 days it is shorter than the cycle itself, so it can never hold two full moons — and some Februaries hold none at all. When that happens, January and March can each go blue in the same year.

sections.heading: The older, stranger definition
body: The original almanac rule counted full moons per season: a season normally gets three, and in a season with four, the third was the blue moon. The simpler month-based rule spread from a mid-century magazine’s mistake and stuck. This site’s list uses the monthly rule and says so on the page — a list that does not name its rule is presenting a choice as a fact.

sections.heading: Has the Moon ever actually been blue?
body: Rarely — and for none of these calendar reasons. After enormous volcanic eruptions or forest fires, ash particles of just the right size scatter red light and let blue through, and the Moon genuinely shows blue-grey: Krakatoa’s 1883 eruption tinted moons around the world for months. The phrase “once in a blue moon,” meaning almost never, is older than either calendar rule — the calendars borrowed the phrase, not the other way round.

question: What are the moon phases called?
shortAnswer: Eight names, in order: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent — then new again, about 29.5 days after the last new. Waxing means growing, waning means shrinking, gibbous means more than half lit, and the quarters are named for the orbit, not the shape.
ledeHtml: Eight names, in order: new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent — and back to new, about 29.5 days after the last one. The words are a small dictionary: waxing is growing, waning is shrinking, a crescent is less than half lit, and gibbous — “humped” — is more than half. The four in-between names describe shapes; the four turning points (new, first quarter, full, last quarter) mark quarters of the journey that causes the shapes.
title: What Are the Moon Phases Called?
description: New moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent — what each name means and how to read tonight’s.
graphicCaption: Where the Moon stands against the Sun right now. That angle is tonight’s phase — the names are just addresses along the lap.
graphicAlt: The Moon on its orbit around Earth, with its position relative to the Sun setting the current phase.

sections.heading: Why “first quarter” looks like a half
body: At first quarter you see a half-lit disc, and the name is still right — it counts the orbit, not the light. The Moon is a quarter of the way around its lap when we see half its lit side. The names track the journey; the shapes track the lighting. Once you know that, “last quarter” stops being confusing too: three-quarters of the way around, the other half lit.

sections.heading: How to read tonight’s moon
body: Two questions identify any phase: how much is lit, and which side is lit. Less than half is a crescent, more than half is gibbous. North of the equator, a moon lit on the right is waxing — heading toward full — and lit on the left is waning; south of the equator the two swap, because you are looking at the same Moon the other way up. Your town’s moon page names tonight’s phase and the 30-day strip shows the whole run.

sections.heading: The same instant, the whole world over
body: The phase is the angle between the Sun and the Moon, so everyone on Earth sees the same phase at the same moment — there is no city where it is first quarter while another has full. What changes with where you stand is which way up the shape hangs, and when the Moon rises. That is why phase pages can be global while moonrise pages have to know your town.

sections.heading: Where the turning points really are
body: New moon is not “no moon” — it is the Moon standing in the Sun’s direction, its lit half facing away from us, up all day and lost in the glare. Full is the opposite station, and it is the only night the Moon is up from sunset to sunrise. Scrub the simulator across a month and you can watch each name arrive as an angle, not as a picture on a calendar.

question: Does the Moon have a dark side?
shortAnswer: No. The Moon has a far side — the half that never faces Earth — but it gets exactly as much sunlight as the side we see. During a new moon, the far side is in full daylight. The “dark” in “dark side” only ever meant unseen, and it stopped being unseen in 1959.
ledeHtml: No — and the two words hiding inside the question are doing different jobs. The Moon has a far side, the half that never faces Earth, because it turns once per orbit. And it has a dark side — whichever half is in night right now — exactly as Earth does. They are only the same half at full moon. At new moon the far side is in full daylight while the face we know is dark. “Dark” only ever meant unseen, and it stopped being unseen in 1959, when the first spacecraft flew around and photographed it.
title: Does the Moon Have a Dark Side?
description: No — the far side of the Moon gets exactly as much sunlight as the side we see. At new moon it is in full daylight. “Dark” only ever meant unseen.
graphicCaption: The Moon right now. Which face points at Earth and which face points at the Sun are two different questions — the picture answers both at once.
graphicAlt: The Moon on its orbit, showing the hemisphere facing Earth and the hemisphere lit by the Sun.

sections.heading: Far is about us; dark is about the Sun
body: “Far side” names a fixed half of the Moon — the same terrain, always turned away from Earth. “Dark side” can only honestly name a moving half: wherever it is currently night, which sweeps right around the Moon every month the same way night sweeps around Earth every day. A fixed name and a moving name can’t be the same thing, and the phases prove it: every crescent you have ever seen is sunlight spilling onto the far side.

sections.heading: Why one side hides at all
body: The Moon spins exactly once per trip around us — not by coincidence, but because Earth’s gravity braked it into step over billions of years, which is tidal locking. So one hemisphere faces us for good. Almost for good: the orbit’s slight ellipse and tilt let us peek a little around the edges — libration — so about 59% of the Moon is visible from Earth over time.

sections.heading: What the far side is actually like
body: Different, not darker. It has almost none of the smooth dark lava plains that make the face we see look like a face — it is paler, more heavily cratered, with a thicker crust, and why the two halves differ so much is still an open question. It is also the quietest radio environment a telescope could ask for, shielded from every transmitter on Earth by 3,500 km of rock, which is why astronomers keep proposing observatories there. The first photographs came from Luna 3 in 1959; the first landing on the far side came sixty years later, in 2019.

question: What is a spring tide?
shortAnswer: A spring tide is the fortnightly run of bigger tides — higher highs, lower lows — that comes when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up at new moon and full moon, so the two pulls add. At the quarter moons they work at right angles and partly cancel: those smaller tides are neap tides. “Spring” has nothing to do with the season; the word means to leap.
ledeHtml: A spring tide is the fortnightly run of bigger tides — higher highs and lower lows — that arrives when the Sun, Moon and Earth stand in a line, so the Sun’s pull adds to the Moon’s. That line-up is exactly what a new moon or a full moon is, which is why the tide range follows the phase. At the quarter moons the Sun pulls at right angles to the Moon and partly cancels it: those smaller tides are neap tides. The season has nothing to do with it — “spring” here is the old sense of the word, to leap up — and the mechanism underneath is what causes tides in the first place.
title: What Is a Spring Tide?
description: Spring tides are the bigger tides at new and full moon, when the Sun’s pull adds to the Moon’s; neap tides are the smaller ones at the quarters. Not the season.
graphicCaption: The two bulges the Moon raises. At new and full moon the Sun’s own, smaller pair lines up with them — spring tides. At the quarters it fights them — neaps.
graphicAlt: Earth with the Moon’s two tidal bulges, showing how the Sun’s alignment strengthens or weakens them.

sections.heading: Twice a month, every month
body: Springs come at both new moon and full moon, because the tides do not care which side of Earth the Moon lines up on — a straight line is a straight line. So the rhythm is: springs, then about seven days later neaps, then springs again, riding the phases all month. It has run at that beat for as long as there has been an ocean.

sections.heading: Read this week’s tides off tonight’s moon
body: This is a genuinely usable trick: look at tonight’s phase. Full or new, and the biggest ranges of the fortnight are landing within a day or two — the ocean lags the alignment slightly. Half-lit, and the week’s tides are at their tamest. Then check the real numbers against your station’s predictions, which solve it properly instead of estimating from the phase.

sections.heading: Why some springs are king tides
body: Not all springs are equal. When the full or new moon also lands near the Moon’s closest approach to Earth — the supermoon coincidence — the two effects stack, and those perigean spring tides are the ones that flood low streets and make the news as king tides.

sections.heading: What the angle looks like from above
body: The whole story is one angle: Sun–Earth–Moon. At 0° and 180° the two tidal stretches align and add; at 90° the Moon’s high water sits on the Sun’s low water. The Sun’s contribution is a bit under half the Moon’s — enormous mass, but tides fall off with the cube of distance, and the Sun is four hundred times farther away. That cube law is also why the nearer, smaller Moon runs the show at all.
